The triangle 2, 3, 5, in the accent color, is the largest set of nodes that are all pairwise connected. The card shows the result [2, 3, 5], size 3." width="100%"} A clique is a set of nodes in which every pair is directly connected. A maximum clique is a largest possible clique in the graph. If multiple maximum cliques exist with the same size, returns one of them (arbitrary choice). Uses the Bron-Kerbosch algorithm to enumerate all maximal cliques and selects the largest. Note the difference between *maximal* and *maximum*: a maximal clique cannot be extended by adding another node, but it need not be the largest one. `find_cliques()` returns every maximal clique; this method returns only a single largest one. Use it when you want the most tightly knit group in a network, for example: - the largest group of people who all know one another in a social network - a densely interacting core of proteins in an interaction network - a set of mutually compatible items (e.g., features or tasks that can all co-occur) If you only need the size of the largest clique, `clique_number()` returns it directly. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Sorted list of node IDs forming a maximum clique. Empty list if graph is empty. In a graph with nodes but no edges, a single node forms the largest clique, so a one-element list is returned. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If called on a directed graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Finding a maximum clique is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard and, in fact, inapproximable within any factor of $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ unless $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{NP}$. This implementation enumerates all maximal cliques via Bron-Kerbosch and returns the largest, which inherits the algorithm's $O(3^{n/3})$ worst-case runtime but performs well on sparse and structured inputs. If more than one maximum clique exists, one is returned arbitrarily. Undirected graphs only; convert a directed graph with `to_undirected()` first if direction does not matter for your question. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a triangle, the maximum clique is the whole graph. The result is a list of node IDs: ::: {#d90eb2ef .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) graph.max_clique() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [1, 2, 3] ``` ::: ::: In a path, no three nodes are mutually connected, so the maximum clique is just a single edge: ::: {#421e4285 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D")]) ) graph.max_clique() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [1, 2] ``` ::: ::: In a small friendship network, "Ann", "Bob", "Cat", and "Dan" all know one another while "Eve" only knows two of them. Mapping the returned IDs back to labels shows the four-person clique: ::: {#11389970 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_nodes(["Ann", "Bob", "Cat", "Dan", "Eve"]) graph.add_edges( [ ("Ann", "Bob"), ("Ann", "Cat"), ("Ann", "Dan"), ("Bob", "Cat"), ("Bob", "Dan"), ("Cat", "Dan"), ("Eve", "Ann"), ("Eve", "Bob"), ] ) [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in graph.max_clique()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['Ann', 'Bob', 'Cat', 'Dan'] ``` ::: ::: An empty graph has no clique to find: ::: {#740e0ced .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph(directed=False).max_clique() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [] ``` ::: ::: In a complete graph, the maximum clique is every node: ::: {#ddb13377 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_full_graph(n=6) len(graph.max_clique()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 6 ``` ::: :::
